sentences.text: Last time, we gave every patient a probability, added them up for Cedar, and got 8 expected readmissions. Cedar had exactly 8.
A perfect match. But a hollow one.
Those probabilities were built from Cedar's own results. We compared Cedar with itself.
To judge a clinic, the expected number has to come from somewhere else.
So the real question is: expected, according to whom?
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: observed, versus expected.
Here's a first idea. Pour all five clinics together: 103 patients.
Sort them by risk, and forget which clinic they came from.
13 of the 57 lower-risk patients were readmitted: 23%.
And 29 of the 46 higher-risk patients: 63%.
Call that the pooled standard: what happens to a typical patient of each kind.
Now take Alder's 30 patients. On the left, what happened to them.
On the right, the slice the standard gives each one.
Add up the slices: 24 small ones and 6 large ones come to about 9.3.
That's Alder's expected count: what these same patients would produce at a typical clinic.
Alder actually had 13.
That's 3.7 more than expected. Or, as a ratio, 13 over 9.3: 1.4.
Now do the same for all five clinics.
Birch had 14, against 16.5 expected: a ratio of 0.85. Fewer than expected.
Remember the league table? Birch's raw rate was higher than Alder's.
Measured against what their own patients were expected to do, Birch comes out ahead.
And notice: the expected counts add up to 42, exactly the number observed.
Against a pooled standard, the clinics as a whole always break even.
It looks like we're done. But look at where that standard came from.
Of the 57 lower-risk patients in the pool, 24 are Alder's own. And they supplied 8 of the 13 readmissions.
Take Alder out, and the lower-risk rate drops from 23% to 15%.
Alder has been measured against a standard it pushed up itself. Against everyone else, its ratio is not 1.4, but 1.8.
There's a second, subtler problem: the risk rule itself.
In the pool, higher risk multiplies the odds by 5.8.
But compare patients inside the same clinic, and the gap is wider: 10 at Alder, 10 at Dune, about 6 at Cedar and at Birch.
Taken together, about seven and a half.
Why the difference? Most higher-risk patients are at Birch, which does well. Most lower-risk patients are at Alder, which doesn't.
The pool mixes up how sick patients are with where they were treated.
Let's gather it up.
Expected is a sum of probabilities, taken over a clinic's own patients.
Observed minus expected is the evidence. Observed over expected is the ratio.
And both are only as fair as the standard behind them.
A fair standard needs two things: a risk rule learned from patients who share a clinic, and a yardstick no single clinic can bend.
Next time, we get both, with one small change: every clinic gets a number of its own.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
